sections.h2: How are Michigan property taxes calculated before you sell?
sections.html:
Michigan assesses property at 50 percent of its true cash value, and that half-value figure is the state equalized value (SEV). Tax is not charged on SEV directly. It is charged on taxable value, which for each parcel is the lesser of two numbers: last year's taxable value (less losses) multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate, whichever is smaller, plus additions, or the current SEV (MCL 211.27a).

This is the Proposal A cap, and it is why two neighboring houses of equal market value can carry very different bills. A long-time owner usually pays on a taxable value well below SEV. A buyer who takes the house usually does not inherit that cushion, which is the single biggest tax fact for anyone selling in Michigan.

  • SEV is half of the assessor's estimate of true cash value.
  • Taxable value grows slowly while the same owner holds the parcel.
  • The millage rate set by each local taxing unit is applied to taxable value to produce the bill.

sections.h2: What happens to taxable value when the house sells?
sections.html:
A transfer of ownership resets taxable value. For the calendar year after the transfer, taxable value becomes the SEV, and the 5-percent-or-inflation cap then applies again from that new base (MCL 211.27a(3) and (4)). The statute defines transfer broadly: a deed, a land contract, certain trust changes, and a distribution under a will or by intestacy all count.

Residential property passing by will or intestacy to a surviving spouse, or to the decedent's parent, child, sibling or grandchild, keeps its capped value, as long as it is not put to commercial use afterward (MCL 211.27a(6)(f)). A land contract is treated as a transfer when it is signed, and the later deed does not trigger a second reset.

The buyer, grantee or other transferee must notify the local assessing office within 45 days of the transfer, on the State Tax Commission form, naming the parties, the transfer date, the actual consideration and the parcel identification number or legal description (MCL 211.27a(10)). The register of deeds also reports recorded transfers to the assessor at least monthly, so the reset happens whether or not the buyer files.

sections.h2: When does the board of review meet, and how do you appeal in Michigan?
sections.html:
The first step is the local board of review. It meets the second Monday in March, and a city or township may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after that as the starting date. The first meeting must begin between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. and run at least six hours, with at least 12 hours across the week and three of those hours after 6 p.m. (MCL 211.30).

An owner or an agent can ask for a corrected assessed or taxable value, and the board must correct it if sufficient cause is shown. A nonresident can protest by letter, and a township or city may also allow resident protests by letter. Written results, with notice of the right to go to the tax tribunal, are due by the first Monday in June.

The Michigan Tax Tribunal hears the next level. Residential, agricultural and timber-cutover real property disputes must be filed by July 31 of the tax year, while commercial, industrial and developmental real property and related personal property petitions are due by May 31. Most other matters carry a 35-day window after the final decision. Residential valuation disputes generally must have been protested at the board of review first. A bill appeal over arithmetic errors has its own 60-day window after the treasurer mails the bill (MCL 205.735a).

sections.h2: How does the principal residence exemption work when you sell?
sections.html:
The principal residence exemption (PRE) removes the local school operating tax from an owner's home. An owner claims it by filing a Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, Form 2368, with the city or township assessor. A claim filed by June 1 reduces taxes from the summer levy, and one filed from June 2 through November 1 reduces them from the winter levy (Treasury PRE claim requirements).

The reverse step matters at sale. When the property stops being the owner's principal residence, the owner must file a Request to Rescind, Form 2602, with the assessor within 90 days. A late filing carries a $5 daily penalty up to $200, and the exemption on the tax roll is removed on December 31 of the year the request is filed.

Other situations follow the same rule. An estate's personal representative or trustee must rescind within 90 days of the owner's death. After a divorce, the spouse who no longer owns and occupies the home files the rescission. After a mortgage foreclosure, the mortgagor files within 90 days of leaving. Forms are available from closing agents, assessors and the Treasury website.

sections.h2: What if the property taxes are not paid?
sections.html:
Township and city treasurers collect the summer and winter bills, and unpaid amounts are then returned to the county treasurer. Summer taxes become a lien and are due July 1, with interest added to anything collected after September 14. Taxes and interest still unpaid before March 1 are returned as delinquent on March 1 (MCL 211.44a).

On a bill paid before February 15 of the following year, a collecting unit may add an administration fee of up to 1 percent. After February 14 and until the taxes are returned as delinquent, a city or township may authorize that fee plus a late penalty of 3 percent (MCL 211.44).

The serious step comes a year later. On March 1, property that has been delinquent for the preceding 12 months or more is forfeited to the county treasurer, with a $175 fee added. The treasurer records a certificate with the register of deeds within 45 days. The owner can redeem by paying the full balance plus extra interest of one-half percent per month, up to the March 31 after the foreclosure judgment, or within 21 days of judgment in a contested case (MCL 211.78g). Anyone selling a house with back taxes should ask the county treasurer for a written payoff well before that date.

sections.h2: What should a Michigan seller check before closing?
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's tax history and work outward. A closing agent will ask for the same items, and gaps are easier to fix before a contract is signed.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer which summer and winter bills are paid, and ask the county treasurer whether any year was returned as delinquent.
  • Confirm the principal residence exemption status with the assessor, and file the rescission within 90 days of moving out.
  • Tell the buyer that taxable value will reset to SEV the year after the sale, so the old bill is not a guide to the new one.
  • If you plan to contest the assessment, note that the March board of review comes first for a residential parcel and the tribunal deadline for it is July 31.
  • For an inherited house, check whether the family-transfer exception keeps the old taxable value before the heirs decide to keep or sell.

Sellers with several years behind should not wait for the forfeiture date. Once a parcel is forfeited, the county treasurer holds it, the foreclosing governmental unit has no right of possession until April 1 after the foreclosure judgment, and redemption closes on the March 31 deadline.

faqs.q: When does the Michigan board of review meet?
faqs.a: On the second Monday in March. A city or township can instead start on the Tuesday or Wednesday that follows, and the board must hold at least 12 hours of sessions that week, including three hours after 6 p.m.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a residential assessment to the Michigan Tax Tribunal?
faqs.a: July 31 of the tax year for residential, agricultural and timber-cutover real property. The assessment generally has to be protested at the board of review first. Commercial and industrial real property petitions are due May 31.

faqs.q: Do Michigan property taxes go up when a house is sold?
faqs.a: Usually yes. A transfer of ownership resets taxable value to the state equalized value for the next calendar year, which removes the Proposal A cap accumulated by the prior owner. The new owner must notify the assessor within 45 days.

faqs.q: How do I remove the principal residence exemption after selling?
faqs.a: File a Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, Form 2602, with the local assessor within 90 days after the property stops being your principal residence. A late filing carries a $5 daily penalty, up to $200.

faqs.q: When does Michigan property go into forfeiture for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: On March 1, once the taxes have been delinquent for the preceding 12 months or more. The property is forfeited to the county treasurer, and the owner can redeem until the March 31 after the foreclosure judgment by paying the full amount due.
